name: Mudu Koraga
confidence_why: No description of Mudu Koraga mentions stress: Bhat (1971), the only first-hand sketch of the dialect, and the KIRTADS Koraga handbook (2019) give only the sound inventory, so the sole indication is Krishnamurti's (2003) family-wide remark that Dravidian languages lack phonemic stress and normally stress the first syllable, which no one has checked for Koraga, while Shetty's Koraga Grammar (1978/2008, Ande dialect) is available only in print and has not been consulted.

catalog_quote: [p. 27, sec. 1.5.1 Phonology] The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants. || [p. 28] Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost. || [p. 27, on the language] Koraga (Bhat 1971) is almost like Tuḷu in most respects and is tentatively shown as an off-shoot of Pre-Tuḷu. || [p. 25, item 12] Koraga. Pop. about 1,000. Basket makers in the South Kanara district. A number of them are bilingual in Tuḷu. It looks more like an off-shoot of Tuḷu at a recent past, although Bhat suggests genetic closeness with North Dravidian (Bhat 1971: 3). || [p. 58, sec. 2.4.1, Google Books snippet, grade snippet] Very little has been written about stress and intonation. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Mudu Koraga, so there is nothing to agree or disagree with; this work adds a family-level statement (non-contrastive, normally initial stress in every Dravidian language) that covers Mudu Koraga only by generalization. Krishnamurti treats Koraga as one language (p. 25, item 12, South Kanara basket makers, off-shoot of Tulu) and the index lists 'Mudu (a dialect of Koraga), 300, 318' (morphology pages: past-stem gemination and personal suffixes, per the Google Books snippet), not phonology. The listed open copy at archive.org (micro_IA41153650_0573) is the ERIC microfiche 'Document Resume' card ED 475 049 -- one page, abstract only, 'Doc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide generalization, not a Mudu Koraga-specific statement: stress is not phonemic in any Dravidian language; it normally falls on the initial syllable of the word whether that syllable is short or long; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (so vowel length carries some prominence outside the initial syllable). Krishnamurti names Koraga as a South Dravidian I language (p. 19, p. 25 entry 12) that is 'almost like Tulu in most respects' (p. 27), but says nothing about Koraga or Mudu stress in particular.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the only related remark is 'A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for the initial-stress generalization. Sec. 2.4.1 (p. 58) opens by saying very little has been written about stress and intonation and cites the Tamil statement of Annamalai and Steever 1998: 104 as 'typical'; the continuation (Andronov 1969: 33 on the place of a stressed syllable) was cut off in the snippet and pp. 58-60 could not be read in full.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti 2003 treats 'Koraga' as a single language (item 12 on p. 25: about 1,000 speakers, South Kanara district, bilingual in Tulu, an off-shoot of Tulu/Pre-Tulu though Bhat 1971: 3 suggested North Dravidian closeness); Mudu appears in the index as 'a dialect of Koraga' at pp. 300 and 318 (verb morphology). The stress statement is about the Dravidian family as a whole and names no Koraga variety.

sources.note: Nothing. Mudu phonology (sec. 1, pp. 33-34) gives only the phonemic inventory, allophony of n and a, distribution/cluster restrictions and minimal-pair contrasts (length, quality, nasalization, gemination, voicing); the Onti (pp. 4-5) and Tappu (pp. 21-22) phonology sections are the same shape. a full-text search for stress/accent both scanned layers for stress/accent/tone/pitch/intonation/prominence: only 'over-emphasized' (p. 3) and 'equal prominence' (p. 23, about canonical shapes of Tappu verbal bases). No stress marks in texts or vocabulary.
